item.title: U.S. threatens "economic D-Day" sanctions on Iran
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
NEW YORK, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday threatened Iran with "an economic D-Day," announcing a wave of new sanctions aimed at further isolating the country. "We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe," said Bessent at a press conference. "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline" that sustains the country, he said. The U.S. Treasury Department said in a press release that the new sectoral sanctions determinations target five critical sectors -- digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping -- that the U.S. says Iran has relied on to prop up its economy. The measures marked the beginning of "a sustained and systematic campaign to close every financial resource" that supports Iran, the department said. It added that "any entity that facilitates money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system." The department is expanding the categories of "Iran-related conduct" that the United States might sanction in the future, and said "every country will be given a defined timeline to shut down the Iran-related activity" the United States has identified. Bessent disclosed that U.S. President Donald Trump has been calling world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with Iran. Simultaneously, the department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels in multiple jurisdictions that enable Iran's activities, including illicit nuclear and missile technology procurement, cyber operations, and oil-revenue generation networks. OFAC also suspended several general licenses that previously authorized certain remittance payments to Iran and Iranian access to the U.S. cultural and academic system. Additionally, the Treasury Department released additional guidance on the sanctions risks associated with complying with Iranian demands regarding shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. In a post on X, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf responded to U.S. economic threats against Tehran by saying that, "Iran's trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don't take these statements into account anywhere." "They cannot cut off our financial lifelines," Iran's Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance Seyed Ali Madanizadeh said in another X post, adding that Tehran has been "planning for some time to counter the sanctions." ■

item.title: China opens exhibition to preserve, bring linguistic diversity to life
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
A visitor listens to dialects of various regions in Hunan at the Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China in Changsha, central China's Hunan Province, Aug. 24, 2026. A new exhibition hall dedicated to the preservation of China's diverse language resources opened on Monday in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, bringing a decade-long effort to document languages and dialects to the public through digital and interactive displays. The Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China, located in the Hunan Museum, brings together recordings and other language materials collected from more than 1,800 field survey sites across China, covering Chinese dialects, ethnic minority languages and related cultural traditions. (Xinhua/Xue Yuge) CHANGSHA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Putting on headphones at a new exhibition hall in central China, visitors can hear a chorus of voices from across the country, including regional dialects, traditional songs in ethnic minority languages and field recordings of languages on the verge of extinction. The Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China opened Monday in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, bringing decade-long efforts to document languages and dialects to the public through digital and interactive displays. Located in the Hunan Museum, the exhibition brings together recordings and other language materials collected from more than 1,800 field survey sites across China. More than 30 language-related cultural relics are also on display. The recordings represent 10 major Chinese dialects and more than 100 ethnic minority languages, including Mongolian, Tibetan, Uygur and Zhuang, said Chen Xuliang, deputy Party secretary of the Hunan Museum. "Digital technology is helping bring the results of language preservation research out of databases and into public cultural spaces," he said. The exhibition draws on materials collected through a national language preservation project launched in 2015 to document and preserve the country's diverse languages and dialects. It is the world's largest project of its kind, according to experts. Over the past decade, researchers have traveled to remote mountain villages and pastoral areas to find native speakers of different ages. They systematically recorded words, grammatical examples, oral traditions and other language materials, turning oral memories at risk of disappearing in digital records that can be preserved for generations. The work has become increasingly urgent as the number of native speakers of some languages declines. China is home to more than 100 languages and numerous dialects. Some languages, including Hezhen and Manchu, now have fewer than 100 speakers. Economic integration, population mobility and the social changes they bring are making it increasingly difficult to preserve languages and cultural traditions around the world, said Wang Lining, a professor at Beijing Normal University's School of Chinese Language and Literature and a participant in the language preservation project. Many languages lack well-developed writing systems, Wang said, meaning knowledge and memories passed down orally can be lost when their speakers die. The new exhibition aims to bring such preservation work closer to the public. It also promotes the principles of the "Yuelu Proclamation," which was officially released in 2019 and described as UNESCO's first permanent document themed on the protection of linguistic diversity. Experts attending the exhibition's opening said a key challenge is how to use artificial intelligence and digital museum technologies to turn vast collections of field recordings into cultural experiences the public can engage with. For Wang, documenting endangered languages is only the beginning. "In the past, the focus was on recording endangered languages and preserving samples of their voices," she said. "In the future, preservation needs to move toward keeping languages alive." The exhibition hall, Wang said, is part of that shift, taking language resources beyond academic research and bringing them closer to everyday life. ■ People visit the Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China in Changsha, central China's Hunan Province, Aug. 24, 2026. item.title: Chinese film turns kitchen into anti-war statement
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
*The film is set in the Middle East, but its emotional center lies elsewhere: in the universal desire to live an ordinary life. *"Don't forget to eat well" is an ordinary phrase in peaceful times. In the film, it becomes something much larger -- a reminder of the normal life that war threatens to take away. *In the movie, the restaurant becomes a small refuge: water, electricity, food, and people from different backgrounds sharing a table while the outside world is held at bay. by Xinhua writers Zhang Yunlong, Xing Tuo and Xiong Jialin BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Xu Fu and Ma Junsheng are asleep when a blast wakes them and for a moment, they think it is an earthquake. Then comes the shockwave, and the understanding that war has arrived. The pivotal scene in Chinese film "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" turns a restaurant kitchen into the center of a story about war, survival and peace. Directed and co-written by Wen Muye, the film follows Xu Fu, a Chinese cook who travels to the Middle East to work in a Chinese restaurant after falling into debt at home. He and restaurant manager Ma Junsheng help build a popular eatery that becomes a gathering place for people of different backgrounds. Then war breaks out. The film opened in Chinese mainland cinemas on Aug. 11. Maoyan, a Chinese ticketing platform, forecasts that the film could gross more than 2.5 billion yuan (about 369 million U.S. dollars) in the Chinese mainland, after it had already taken in around 1.6 billion yuan by Monday. The film has also received a rating of 8.6 on Douban, a major review platform. The film's appeal lies less in its explosion scenes, than in what happens between them. WHY FOOD Wen said the decision to tell a war story through a restaurant came from a simple contrast: war is cruel, while food represents happiness. The film returns repeatedly to cooking, from dumplings prepared before Xu leaves home to a wedding banquet where Chinese and Arab food traditions meet. Later, fleeing the fighting with a group of orphaned children, Xu prepares a simple pot of rice. The meal is modest, Wen said, but it gives the children a sense of safety. The dish eventually becomes known as "Xu Fu Rice Stew" at the restaurant. The film is set in the Middle East, but its emotional center lies elsewhere: in the universal desire to live an ordinary life. "Don't forget to eat well" is an ordinary phrase in peaceful times. In the film, it becomes something much larger -- a reminder of the normal life that war threatens to take away. RESTAURANT IN RUINS The restaurant setting reflects a familiar reality in the history of Chinese migration. For decades, opening restaurants has been one of the most common ways for Chinese migrants to make a living overseas. The film's Loong Restaurant is rooted in a real story. Shuai Xuejun, from Jiangxi Province, traveled to Iraq in 2004 at age 31 and opened a restaurant of the same name with friends in Baghdad, in a run-down building with broken windows and no proper door. The restaurant eventually grew into a thriving business, employing about 20 people and generating daily revenue of 4,000 to 5,000 U.S. dollars at its peak. But the noise of the restaurant could not keep out the war. One morning, Shuai was woken by a blast that shook dust loose from the walls; the bomb had exploded about three kilometers away. What stayed with him the longest, he said, was not the sound of explosions but small acts of kindness. A regular customer helped him replace a malfunctioning television for recreation when the store was closed during the war. When Shuai finally left Iraq in March 2005, another regular customer told him: "When you leave, there will be no Chinese flavor here." Shuai and his colleagues later wrote a book about their experiences. A film company acquired the rights years later. MORE THAN FOOD The film resonates with the people who have lived through war themselves. Ahmed Mohammed Jaber Alkalthoom, an Iraqi-born actor who appears briefly in the film, is better known in China as a food blogger. Born in Iraq in 1994, Jaber grew up amid conflict. He later recalled once mistaking the sound of missiles for fireworks. He moved to China with his family in 2014 and began filming Chinese food in 2018. In 2024, while filming a video during the Chinese New Year holiday, he froze at the sound of a firecracker. "I thought it was a bomb," he recalled. Viewers who saw the footage left messages reassuring him: "Don't be afraid. This is China." "During wartime, there would be no water or electricity. A family would take out the food they had hidden and share it, and that felt warm and healing," he said. For him, being able to eat well became part of everyday Chinese life -- something he still regards as "a great thing." WAR STORY WITHOUT SUPER HERO The film also stands apart from more conventional action-driven war stories. Xu Fu is not a conventional hero. Going abroad to earn money and pay off debt, he is an ordinary man whose life is gradually transformed as the war forces him to confront the fate of those around him. Ma Junsheng, who is more idealistic, ultimately sacrifices himself protecting children. Saif, an orphan who initially steals food to survive, gradually learns to cook under Xu's guidance. Egyptian journalist Mohamed Mazen, who has lived in China for 17 years, said he did not feel the usual distance he associates with Chinese cinema while watching the film. Its questions about war, food and ordinary life, he said, cross cultural boundaries. Mazen said he was struck by the film's perspective on war. Having grown up watching Hollywood films, he was accustomed to stories centered on soldiers, rescuers and larger-than-life heroes. In contrast, he said, "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" focuses on cooks, restaurant workers and children trying to preserve a sense of normality amid violence. In the movie, the restaurant becomes a small refuge: water, electricity, food, and people from different backgrounds sharing a table while the outside world is held at bay. Years later, Xu Fu returns to the region as a tourist. Finding the Loong Restaurant again, he discovers that Saif, the orphan who he once taught to cook, has become its head chef. The boy who grew up in war has chosen a life in the kitchen, with a spatula in his hand rather than a gun -- a quiet ending to a film that measures the cost of war not only in lives lost, but in the ordinary life people struggle to preserve. (Video reporter: Xu Haofu, Yao Bing, Dong Xiuzhu and Zhang Yanfang; video editors: Liang Wanshan, Roger Lott and Zheng Qingbin)■

item.title: Xi calls on China, Jordan to further deepen alignment of development strategies
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Chinese President Xi Jinping holds talks with King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein, who is on a state visit to China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Xiang) BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- China and Jordan should further deepen the alignment of development strategies, Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Monday. Both sides should enhance cooperation in traditional fields including economy and trade, infrastructure construction, transportation and mining, expand new drivers of cooperation in digital economy, artificial intelligence and green energy, and comprehensively deepen exchanges in education, culture, science and technology, tourism and other areas, Xi said when holding talks with King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein in Beijing. Xi noted that in 2015, the two heads of state jointly announced the establishment of China-Jordan strategic partnership, opening a new chapter in the development of bilateral relations. Facing an international and regional situation characterized by intertwined changes and chaos, building a more substantive and dynamic China-Jordan relationship is in line with the common expectations of the two peoples and also conforms to the general trend of the pursuit of the Global South for strength through unity, he said. Xi emphasized that China attaches great importance to Jordan's unique and significant role in the region, firmly supports Jordan in safeguarding its national sovereignty, security and development interests, and is willing to maintain close exchanges with Jordan at all levels including the governments, political parties, legislative bodies and localities, and enhance exchanges of experience in governance. China is willing to work with Jordan to implement the four major global initiatives, enhance coordination and cooperation in multilateral institutions including the United Nations, jointly safeguard the international system with the United Nations at its core and the international order underpinned by international law, and promote the building of a community with a shared future for humanity, Xi said. King Abdullah II said Jordan and China have established a strong strategic partnership, with fruitful cooperation across various fields. He said Jordan firmly upholds the one-China policy and regards Taiwan as part of China's territory. Jordan places high priority on its relations with China and is dedicated to expanding cooperation and exchanges in economy and trade, manufacturing, agriculture, science and technology, pharmaceuticals, culture and education, King Abdullah II said, adding that Jordan welcomes more Chinese enterprises to invest there to achieve common development and prosperity. Jordan speaks highly of the four global initiatives put forward by President Xi and looks forward to China's greater leading role on the global stage, King Abdullah II said. After the talks, the two heads of state jointly attended a signing ceremony for multiple cooperation documents in areas such as diplomacy, economy and trade, industrial and supply chains, and justice. The two sides also issued a joint statement on deepening the strategic partnership between China and Jordan. Prior to the talks in the Great Hall of the People, Xi held a welcome ceremony for King Abdullah II. Xi also hosted a welcome banquet for him in the evening. ■ Chinese President Xi Jinping holds a welcome ceremony for King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein in the Northern Hall of the Great Hall of the People prior to their talks in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 24, 2026. item.title: IPO, athletic feats and mass deployment show China's robot momentum
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The past week has been busy and fruitful for China's humanoild robot industry, which is qucikly racing from lab demos toward real-world deployment. On Wednesday, as the 2026 World Robot Conference (WRC) opened in Beijing, drawing more than 300 exhibitors from 26 countries with over 3,000 products, Unitree Robotics became the first humanoid robot maker to list on China's A-share market. On Saturday, the second World Humanoid Robot Games kicked off at the "Ice Ribbon," the 2022 Winter Olympics venue, with 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries. ROAD TO PROFITABILITY Unitree debuted on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's STAR Market on Aug. 19, opening at 1,100 yuan (about 162 U.S. dollars) per share -- a 629-percent premium. As of Monday's opening, although it had pulled back significantly, it still remained at a high level. The sell-off from the opening high was a sobering signal. Financial observers noted that the sector will enter a digestion period that may last for months, predicting investors will shift their focus from rewarding "the only listed robot stock" to its actual business performance. Still, Unitree's listing marks a watershed moment for China's humanoid robot industry. The listing will transition the industry from "technological validation" and "narrative-driven hype" into an era of "commercial value verification," where profitability is the ultimate test, said Tian Lihui, a finance professor at Nankai University. Unitree has already delivered a compelling answer. Established in 2016, the company shipped over 5,500 humanoid units in 2025 to secure the top spot worldwide. Its revenue surged to nearly 1.7 billion yuan in 2025, and the momentum continued into the first half of 2026, with revenue reaching approximately 1.15 billion yuan, up 48.54 percent year on year. Unitree's success is underpinned by its strong emphasis on independent R&D and technological innovation. The company has achieved vertical integration by developing proprietary core components -- including motors, reducers, controllers, and LiDAR -- alongside high-performance perception and motion control algorithms. This in-house approach is backed by a portfolio of over 200 patent applications. The company's founder Wang Xingxing attributed its growth to independent innovation, pragmatic execution and long-termism. He emphasized that, because the humanoid robotics industry remains in its dawn phase, navigating its significant challenges requires collective effort and sustained investment from the entire sector. TECH LEAP IN PITCH While the IPO measured progress in valuation, the robot games measured it in velocity, endurance and raw athleticism -- taking the technology off the lab bench and onto the pitch. In the 100-meter heats, the Beijing-based humanoid robot Tien Kung Ultra crossed in 9.39 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt's 9.58-second human world record. Tien Kung Ultra also posted a standing high jump of 2.88 meters, well above the human mark. The games also featured a dazzling array of human-machine showdowns: robots traded shots with Olympic table tennis champion Ding Ning and tennis Grand Slam winner Zheng Jie, and went toe-to-toe with former national football player Yang Chen. Robot football offered a special glimpse of how far the technology has come. Beijing-based Booster Robotics' newly developed bipedal robot, Booster T2, is the star player in the large size group of the football tournament at this year's games. Beyond its taller stature and greater strength, the robot can kick balls at over 100 km/h, and its end-side computing power is 10 times that of the previous generation, with the system latency dropping from 10 milliseconds to 4 milliseconds. Many events at the games were run fully autonomously, with no remote controls, testing robots' ability to perceive and decide independently. "Every centimeter higher, every kilogram heavier, reflects engineers' optimization of joint motors and reducers," said Jiang Guangzhi of Beijing's Bureau of Economy and Information Technology. REAL-WORLD APPLICATIONS As China's robots demonstrate formidable technological prowess, the industry is now focusing on expanding robots' real-world applications -- a widely recognized challenge within the industry. The World Robot Conference serves as a resounding testament to China's pragmatic shift and its global resonance. At the event, Beijing Galbot Co., Ltd. drew crowds with robots folding clothes, fetching goods, and making breakfast. The company says its pharmacy sorting robots are already deployed in nearly 100 stores across more than 10 cities, including Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. At the Galaxea AI display area, visitors could scan a QR code to place an order and then watch a wheeled robot pick, pack and label items they ordered in real time. The company's robots will be rolled out to unmanned warehouses and supermarkets this year, and has already partnered with JD.com for warehouse sorting and shelving. Practical robots took center stage, just as the Spanish news agency Agencia EFE reported on the conference, Chinese companies are transitioning robots from mere "attention-grabbers" to genuine "workers and practical consumer goods." Xiong Youjun, CEO of the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, said this year's conference showed an industry clearly transitioning from mere technological showmanship to industrial implementation. He added that the sector is currently on the "eve of the ChatGPT moment" regarding embodied intelligence, with companies across the board accelerating the deployment and validation of their technologies. A recent Morgan Stanley report draws a striking parallel between the current trajectory of China's humanoid robotics industry and the electric vehicle sector a decade ago. The investment bank predicts that over the next five to ten years, humanoid robots are poised to become the next major driver of China's machinery exports. BOOMING INDUSTRIAL LANDSCAPE The rapid ascent of the robot industry perfectly aligns with China's national strategic blueprint for future development. "Embodied intelligence" was first written into China's government work report in 2025. Furthermore, China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for a forward-looking layout of future industries, including embodied artificial intelligence, alongside mechanisms to boost funding and share risks in these emerging sectors. Data underscores this momentum. Among companies currently queuing for an IPO on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange alone, 46 are robotics-related, highlighting China's systematic industrial advantage in embodied AI. As Bloomberg noted, the surge in robot IPOs "reflects the rapid rise of China's AI ecosystem." This wave of listings comes amid China's robotics sector securing unprecedented global prominence. China is now home to over 140 humanoid robot manufacturers. With an annual shipment volume of 14,400 units, the country now accounts for eight out of every ten humanoid robots produced globally. Global shipments of humanoid robots reached approximately 19,100 units in the first half of this year, with China accounting for over 97 percent of the global total, industry data shows. According to Xi Yue, co-founder of Beijing-based leading robot maker Robotera, the nation's robotics industry now stands firmly in the first tier globally, boasting the world's largest application market, the most comprehensive supply chain, and a leading edge in embodied AI algorithms. ■

item.title: Xi congratulates Alamgir on assuming Bangladeshi presidency
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Monday extended congratulations to Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on assuming the office as president of Bangladesh. In his congratulatory message, Xi noted China and Bangladesh are traditional friendly neighbors. Xi said that since the establishment of diplomatic ties 51 years ago, the two countries have enjoyed mutual respect, treated each other as equals, supported each other on issues of their respective core interests and major concerns, and joined hands on their paths towards modernization. Bilateral relations have withstood the tests of a rapidly changing international situation, Xi said. Xi said he attaches great importance to the development of China-Bangladesh relations, and is willing to work with Alamgir to carry forward the traditional friendship, strengthen strategic communication, advance high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, deepen exchanges and cooperation in all fields, and guide the building of a China-Bangladesh community with a shared future in the new era to go deeper and more solid, so as to better benefit the two peoples. ■

item.title: Xi puts forward four principles on Palestinian question
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Chinese President Xi Jinping holds talks with King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein, who is on a state visit to China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Xiang) BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping stressed on Monday that four principles should be followed to push for the resolution of the Palestinian question, which is at the heart of the Middle East issue. Xi made the remarks in talks with King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein in Beijing. First, a political settlement should be upheld. The two-state solution is the right direction, and efforts should be made to restart peace talks between Palestine and Israel, with a view to establishing an independent Palestinian state at an early date, Xi said. Second, the principle of "Palestinians governing Palestine" should be followed in advancing the governance of the West Bank and the post-war reconstruction of Gaza, he said. Third, humanitarian principles must be upheld. The international community, and the UN Security Council in particular, should shoulder its responsibility effectively to protect civilian safety, ensure the flow of humanitarian assistance, and put an end to humanitarian disasters, Xi said. Fourth, fairness and justice must be upheld. This means following international law, addressing both symptoms and root causes, and taking practical actions so that the Palestinian question can be resolved in a comprehensive, just and lasting way at an early date, he said. On the Middle East situation, Xi said China has always advocated a comprehensive ceasefire and end of hostilities, and resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means, adding that the sovereignty and security of Jordan and all other countries in the region should be respected. Noting Jordan appreciates China's impartial stance on Middle East affairs and its support for the just cause of Arab countries, King Abdullah II said Jordan is ready to maintain close communication with China and continue to make active efforts for de-escalation. ■

item.title: Xi stresses consolidating, expanding campaign on correct view of governance performance
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, has emphasized the importance of consolidating and expanding the progress made in a Party-wide study and education campaign for establishing and practicing a correct understanding of governance performance. Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction, which was studied at a meeting of the CPC Central Leading Group for Party Building held on Monday. Xi stressed that establishing and putting into practice a correct view of governance performance is a long-term task that requires sustained efforts. Since the 18th CPC National Congress, the organization of study and education campaigns across the Party to address major and pressing issues in Party building has become an important institutional arrangement, Xi said, lauding the notable results achieved in the latest campaign. Xi emphasized the need to regularly conduct education on the correct view of governance performance, guiding Party members and officials to always take responsibility, perform their duties and fulfill their obligations in accordance with such a view. Efforts should also be made to improve differentiated assessment and evaluation systems, and establish a personnel selection and appointment orientation that values solid work and concrete results, Xi said. During the meeting, participants thoroughly studied and implemented Xi's instruction, reviewed the campaign, and made arrangements for consolidating and expanding the campaign's outcomes and establishing a long-term mechanism accordingly. The meeting was chaired by Cai Qi, who is head of the CPC Central Leading Group for Party Building, and was also attended by Li Xi, the group's deputy head. Cai and Li, both of whom are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, also delivered speeches. The meeting noted that the campaign has resolved prominent issues related to deviations in view of governance performance, regulated the official conduct of leading officials at all levels, and given a strong boost to all work aimed at ensuring a good start to the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The campaign, which started in late February, has basically concluded and aimed to correct misguided views on governance that often breed vanity projects, hidden risks, heavy burdens on local communities, and public discontent. ■
